statements.t: Oklo stands apart from the legacy nuclear industry – we will primarily own and operate our powerhouses and directly sell our power to customers, rather than licensing our designs for others to build and operate.
We are incentivized to design, build, and operate more efficiently because we will bear the costs of creating and operating our powerhouses.

The Aurora Powerhouse product line is expected not just to broaden our customer base, but also to provide shorter construction cycles and more frequent deployments – each an opportunity to learn and improve with the next project.

Despite the distinct technical requirements across our suite of projects, there can be significant learnings related to construction, procurement, instrumentation, regulatory licensing pathways, and nuclear and non-nuclear operations.

We are also developing fuel recycling technology and aim to build facilities that can unlock the abundant residual energy in the U.S.’s large stock of used nuclear fuel, while also potentially recovering valuable isotope materials.
Our business advances in stages and we aim to develop this ecosystem through investments that build on each other.
We believe that a strong ecosystem for nuclear energy will enable each of power, fuel fabrication, recycling and isotopes to achieve their respective business objectives.
We estimate that the existing energy reserves contained in the used nuclear fuel in the U.S. that could be made accessible through our fast fission reactor technology.

Other regulatory approvals, including the OTA and receipt of the Environmental Compliance Permit, have further advanced our plans to deliver the first commercial advanced fission power plant in the U.S.

To this end, the Company is expanding its capabilities in precision manufacturing, prototyping, and chemical process engineering through recent acquisitions in support of its power projects, as well as its fuel and isotopes projects.

In May 2026, we announced a strategic partnership project with Battelle Energy Alliance, the management and operating contractor for INL, to integrate INL’s Prometheus AI platform with our multiphysics design and analysis infrastructure to support AI-enabled engineering workflows, model benchmarking and validation, technical documentation, and development of Pluto.
These collaborations are intended to improve engineering efficiency and advance our reactor and fuel-system development activities while supporting the broader objectives of the Genesis Mission.
Our fuel strategy is intended to combine external supply arrangements with the development of our own fuel fabrication and recycling capabilities.

In September 2025, we announced plans to design, build, and operate a fuel recycling facility in Tennessee as the first phase of an advanced fuel center (the "Advanced Fuel Center") to recycle used nuclear fuel into fuel for fast reactors, including our Aurora powerhouse line.

The facility, which includes a roadmap of up to $1.68 billion in investment, will be the first of its kind in the U.S. and we estimate that it has the potential to create more than 800 high-quality jobs.
We have completed a licensing project plan for the fuel recycling facility with the NRC and are currently in pre-application engagement with the regulator’s staff.
Fuel is a significant input to enable us to build and operate our powerhouses at scale and generate expected returns.
These efforts are part of our integrated nuclear strategy, creating opportunities to supply valuable products while building capabilities that support our power and fuel projects.

The project also required us to build and exercise capabilities across private-site development, nuclear safety analysis, quality assurance, commercial procurement, construction, commissioning, operator training and qualification, radiation protection, security, emergency preparedness, DOE readiness review, startup, and operations.

In our differentiated build, own, and operate business model, we plan to sell power in the forms of electricity and heat directly to customers, which we believe can allow for fast-tracked customer adoption and broader market opportunities.
Together, we aim to meet the increasing demands for radioisotopes in medical, energy, industry, defense, and artificial intelligence applications.
The primary product for our power business will be the energy produced from our Aurora powerhouses once operational.

Selling power through PPAs is a common practice within the renewable energy and utility sectors and indicates that this business model could be feasible for power plants within the size range targeted by our Aurora product line ( i.e. , 15 MWe-75 MWe, and ranging upward to potential sizes of 100 MWe and higher).
We plan to be the designer, builder, owner, and operator of our powerhouses and plan to focus on small-scale powerhouses (15 MWe-75 MWe, and potentially 100 MWe and higher).

We expect this approach to enable us to reduce and manage lifecycle regulatory and operating costs in an integrated fashion over time, as opposed to the historical model used in the nuclear power industry, which divides the incentives and responsibilities between the developer and the utility.

Additionally, this modular and scalable approach enables us to better deal with the inherent uncertainties, costs, and inefficiencies of the many service providers, manufacturers, fuel providers, and other third parties that we will rely on to build our powerhouses.

While we expect that individual powerhouses may, and our first few powerhouses likely will, experience challenges that require us to manage unexpected costs and possible construction delays, our business model allows us to take the learnings from constructing those powerhouses and make improvements with future projects.

In particular, we expect the construction of our first powerhouse projects, including the Aurora-ID, to include investments that support both initial deployment and the development of our broader powerhouse fleet.

Certain investments are specific to the capabilities planned for INL and are not expected to be required at each subsequent powerhouse, while other costs are expected to decline as we reuse designs, refine construction methods, and apply experience from initial deployments.
Although these capabilities add cost and complexity to the initial project, we expect them to support improvements in subsequent
We also expect opportunities to reduce costs through design optimization and standardization, repeat procurement, and more efficient construction execution.

While this model is more typically used for renewable energy solutions, we believe it is a compelling model for us because of the relatively small size and the lower expected capital costs of our powerhouses, when compared with other nuclear power plants.
Our powerhouses could be operating cash flow positive from the first year of operation due to our anticipated favorable unit economics.
We also believe this approach will drive unit growth and allow us to ultimately launch higher output versions of our powerhouses.
As our technology matures, we intend to offer customers flexibility in business model and deployment solutions to meet their needs, providing us with the largest target customer base possible.

Given our growth stage, we continue to develop and evaluate our overall cost and potential pricing structure as we evaluate our unit economics, which we expect to be subject to market and extrinsic forces such as the impact of construction costs as a result of tariffs, supply chain pressures, and other macroeconomic factors.

In addition to selling power under PPAs, we are taking steps to enhance our mission with our fuel fabrication projects and advanced nuclear fuel recycling technology as well as executing targeted acquisitions to build capabilities to support our businesses.

On October 13, 2026, we announced plans to advance Groves-2 Forge, an isotope production and processing pilot facility, through the DOE’s National Reactor Innovation Center Nuclear Energy Launch Pad initiative.

Groves-2 Forge is planned to build on our experience developing and operating the Groves Isotope Test Reactor under DOE authorization by integrating reactor irradiation with hot-cell processing, including isotope separation and product recovery, and capabilities for packaging and transportation.

We intend to use these integrated capabilities to prepare isotope products and generate operating experience to support the planned transition of Groves-2 Forge from pilot operations to commercial-scale production, subject to obtaining the appropriate NRC licenses for commercial operation.

We plan to leverage the next-generation fast fission powerhouses that we are developing in order to sell power to a variety of potential customers, including data centers, military and other government facilities, factories, industrial customers, off-grid and remote communities, commercial and institutional campuses, and utilities.

We are evaluating the timing and form of future NRC applications in light of evolving federal policy, NRC rulemaking, and implementation guidance, including the recently finalized Part 53 framework and proposed Part 57 framework.

We intend to use applicable safety analyses, testing results, and operating experience developed through the DOE authorization and operation of Aurora-ID to support subsequent NRC licensing of Aurora-ID and future Aurora deployments.
We believe this framework could reduce duplicative technical reviews and improve licensing efficiency.
It is uncertain when, if at all, we will obtain NRC approvals for the design, construction, and operation of any of our powerhouses.

Our financial condition, commercial plans, and results of operations are likely to be materially and adversely affected if we do not obtain such approvals or if this process takes significantly longer or costs more than we expect.
Additionally, we plan to be the designer, builder, owner, and operator of our powerhouses and plan to focus on small-scale powerhouses (15 MWe, 75 MWe, and potentially 100 MWe and higher designs).

We expect this approach to enable us to reduce and manage lifecycle regulatory and operating costs in an integrated fashion, as opposed to the historical model used in the nuclear power industry, which divides the incentives and responsibilities between the developer and the utility.

The global supply chain on which we will rely (including for HALEU), has been significantly impacted in recent years by inflation, instability in the banking sector, war and other hostilities, and other economic uncertainties, resulting in potential significant delays and cost fluctuations.

Our initial assets in operation will represent the first deployment of our Aurora design and, as such, will be subject to risk around both cost and time associated with first-of-a-kind capital project delivery.
In particular, we expect the construction of our first powerhouse at INL to include additional, unique costs as compared to the costs expected for future powerhouse projects.
We expect future powerhouses to benefit from substantial cost reductions as compared to our first reactor deployment.

To further our ambitious target of deploying our first powerhouse in 2028-2029 and support subsequent powerhouse deployments and the development of our fuel and isotope businesses, amidst a range of supply chain, geopolitical, macroeconomic, and design complexities, we plan to pursue the following key initiatives:
("Kiewit"), who was selected as the lead constructor for our first Aurora powerhouse in Idaho, a major milestone toward project delivery and execution.

We will begin site preparation for other announced projects based on prioritization, potentially including prospective customers such as Meta, Equinix, Diamondback Energy, Prometheus Hyperscale, Switch, and other future projects.

• Progressing production of radioisotopes by our isotope business, assessing options to scale production, and developing and executing plans to grow this business, including developing plans for our Groves-2 Forge project.

We expect our total cash used in operating activities for 2026 to be in the range of $120 million to $150 million and our total cash used for purchases of property, plant and equipment to be in the range of $400 million to $500 million.
Additionally, opponents of advanced nuclear deployments in the U.S. and intervenors in regulatory proceedings could delay the licensing that our business model requires.

We have several recycling technology projects awarded as R&D cost-share projects (the “cost-share projects”) through the DOE’s Advanced Research Projects Agency – Energy (“ARPA-E”) and the DOE Technology Commercialization Fund (“TCF”).
The ARPA-E and TCF projects involve cost-sharing of project costs as well as reimbursement of certain qualifying expenditures to us.

estimates.name: Emerging Growth Company Status
estimates.t: The Company is classified as an emerging growth company (“EGC”), as defined under the Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act (the “JOBS Act”).
